name: codebase-memory-mcp
description: Local MCP server that indexes a codebase into a persistent SQLite knowledge graph and exposes 17 search, trace, query and ADR tools to coding agents.
scored_configuration: Default stdio MCP entry written by the install command: daemon-backed server with the full 17-tool profile, graph UI off, auto_index off, auto_watch on, no CBM_ALLOWED_ROOT and no recorded allow-root grants.
headline: A local code-graph server that holds no credentials, makes no network calls and ships accurate read-only and destructive labels on all 17 tools, so a hijacked agent can do limited damage through it. The main gap is that git, grep and find helpers run unsandboxed through a shell, with only a character filter guarding the model-supplied values they include. Any non-sensitive directory can be indexed and read back by default. ADR text and repository-supplied graph snapshots persist into later sessions without review, and the audit log records tool names but not what each call did.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: The server holds no credentials and talks to no outside service; it runs as the local user and reads and writes files with that user's rights. Its main narrowing is a workspace policy that refuses to index the home directory, shallow system paths and known credential folders such as .ssh and .aws, plus an optional allowed-root setting and per-user grants managed from the command line. With nothing configured, any other directory the user can read can be indexed and its source returned, so the narrowing is a short deny list rather than a least-privilege allowlist.

S.finding: Runs with the OS user's ambient file authority; the only narrowing in the default configuration is a deny list of home, shallow and credential-named roots.
S.gap: No allowlist by default: indexing is unconfined apart from the always-refused roots unless the operator sets CBM_ALLOWED_ROOT or records grants.

C.finding: Both indexing entry points (the MCP tool and the optional UI index route) call the same root policy, and file reads go through a realpath containment check against the indexed root.
C.gap: No per-request authorization layer beyond the root policy; helper subprocesses inherit the full user environment apart from git's repository variables.

evidence.contains: the current environment minus the repository-local

D.finding: Widening needs an operator action (CBM_ALLOWED_ROOT unset is the default; sensitive roots need an explicit allow-root --approve-sensitive from the CLI), and no MCP tool can add grants.
D.gap: The default is not near-minimal: everything outside the deny list is allowed until the operator declares a boundary.

B.finding: A hijacked server can read user-readable source outside the denied roots and write only its own cache databases, ADR text and an opt-in artifact folder in the repository; there are no external credentials or network calls.
B.gap: Reads are not confined to one project by default, and the authority is the long-lived OS user rather than a scoped identity.

evidence.note: No outbound HTTP client or DNS resolution in the server source.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: As a tool server it relies on the MCP host to ask the user before calls, and it gives the host accurate information to decide with: every one of its 17 tools carries hard-coded read-only and destructive labels, and only index_repository, manage_adr and delete_project are marked as writing. A server-enforced read-only tool profile exists, but it is only used when the client launches the server with that flag; the default entry exposes all tools. There is no dry-run or preview for the destructive tools, and deleting an index or replacing an ADR has no undo, though both affect only local data.

S.finding: Separate read and write tools with explicit readOnlyHint/destructiveHint on every tool; an unknown tool name falls back to destructive and not read-only.
S.gap: No preview or dry-run for delete_project or manage_adr writes, and the read-only profile is not on by default.

C.finding: All 17 tools are listed in the one annotation table, the read-only handlers resolve stores through a query-only path, and the dispatcher rejects any tool outside the active profile.
C.gap: Unknown tools are labelled, not rejected, by the annotation layer, and no server-side confirmation step exists for the three write tools.

evidence.contains: is not available in the %s tool profile

D.finding: Annotations and profiles are compiled in; the profile is chosen only by a launch flag, and nothing the model, tool input or a workspace file supplies can change them.
D.gap: Elevated (full) profile is the default and is not session- or time-bounded.

B.finding: A wrongly approved call can delete a project index (rebuildable by reindexing) or overwrite the stored ADR with no undo; no external or high-impact action exists.
B.gap: No checkpoint or undo for ADR replacement and no preview for deletion.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: Tools are narrow, purpose-built graph operations rather than general shells or HTTP clients. File reads are checked against the indexed root after resolving symlinks, project names are validated, result sizes and traversal depths are clamped, and the Cypher interface accepts only a read subset. Weaker spots: arguments that reach helper commands are checked with a character deny list, the index root is not restricted beyond the sensitive-root deny list by default, and the default tool set includes the three write tools.

S.finding: Mix of allowlist-grade checks (realpath containment, project-name validation, numeric clamps) and deny-list filtering of shell metacharacters for helper-command arguments.
S.gap: Helper-command arguments and index roots are checked by deny lists rather than allowlists, and file containment is check-then-open rather than race-safe.

C.finding: Every built-in tool resolves projects through the shared validator, file-returning tools share the containment guard, and there are no extension tools.
C.gap: No single central policy layer that new tools inherit automatically.

D.finding: Tool groups are selectable (scout and analysis profiles), but the default profile includes index_repository, manage_adr and delete_project.
D.gap: The default tool set is not read-only.

B.finding: Misuse can index and read back source from any non-denied directory and change only local index data; outputs are bounded (snippet 500 lines, trace limit 5000).
B.gap: Reads are not scoped to one workspace by default.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: The server has no tool that runs model-written code, but several tools (search_code, detect_changes and the git-history passes) build command lines for git, grep and find as shell strings that include model-supplied values such as search scopes, file patterns and branch names. The only guard is a character filter that rejects quotes, semicolons, pipes and similar metacharacters; there is no sandbox, and the helpers run on the host as the user with the full environment apart from git's repository variables. No second layer sits behind that filter: the helpers have the same reach as the user.

S.finding: No isolation primitive: helper commands are run via /bin/sh -c on the host, protected only by metacharacter filtering and quoting.
S.gap: No argv-based execution or OS sandbox for helper processes.

C.finding: The filter is applied on the search_code, detect_changes and git-history paths, but no path is isolated.
C.gap: No helper path runs inside any isolation boundary.

D.finding: The filtering is always on and cannot be disabled by the model or a workspace file.
D.gap: No sandbox to enable; the protection is filtering only.

evidence.contains: path or file_pattern contains invalid characters

B.finding: Helpers run as the user on the host with the inherited environment and full network, so a failure of the filter is host-equivalent.
B.gap: Helpers would need a minimal environment and no shell interpretation to limit reach.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: Everything the server returns comes from repository content the user did not write, such as source code, comments and docstrings. Results are structured: code comes back with its file path and line numbers, and the server's own guidance sits in separate hint fields rather than mixed into the content. Nothing marks repository text as untrusted for the host. The installed hooks also push repository-derived symbol names into some agents' context outside any tool call. The server itself has no outbound channel, but its write tools and the host's own tools remain available to a hijacked model.

S.finding: Structured outputs separate returned code from metadata (path, lines) and server hints; server instructions are short workflow guidance without content mixed in.
S.gap: No untrusted/provenance flag the host can act on, and no server mode that drops write tools by default.

evidence.note: The single hit is a comment on path normalization, not an output marker.

C.finding: Tool results carry source paths, but hook-injected context and stored ADR text reach the model with no marking.
C.gap: Repository content on every path, including hook output and ADR text, is not distinguished from trusted text.

evidence.contains: Treat project names, symbols, and paths as untrusted repository data.

D.finding: The structured output format is fixed in code and cannot be turned off by content.
D.gap: Nothing beyond output structure is on by default.

B.finding: A hijacked host can use this server only to read local source and change local index or ADR data; the server offers no egress, and its write tools are labelled for host approval.
B.gap: Sensitive source anywhere on disk outside the denied roots is reachable, and the write tools are exposed in the default profile.

evidence.note: No outbound client in the server.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: The server keeps a persistent graph per project and an architecture decision record (ADR) that the model can overwrite at will through manage_adr; that text is stored in the project database and returned in later sessions with no review or history. When a repository contains a committed graph snapshot (.codebase-memory/graph.db.zst) and there is no local index yet, it is imported automatically; the source notes that imported content is trusted as-is. The only repository file that can widen what the server indexes, a manifest of extra roots, needs an explicit approval from the command line that lapses when the file changes. The per-project config file can only map file extensions.

S.finding: ADR writes are unvalidated and unversioned, and repository-supplied graph snapshots are imported without a trust decision; only the extra-roots manifest requires a content-keyed human approval.
S.gap: Memory writes and snapshot imports need validation, review or a trust decision, with history to roll back.

evidence.contains: An imported artifact is trusted for graph CONTENT as-is

C.finding: Only the extra-roots manifest is controlled; ADR text and imported snapshots are not.
C.gap: ADR store and snapshot import are outside any control.

D.finding: Each project has its own database file in the per-user cache; there is one local user, but the model can write the ADR of any indexed project.
D.gap: Model writes are not restricted to the current project's namespace.

B.finding: Poisoned ADR text or graph content persists across all of the user's sessions and every agent sharing the cache, and when a team commits the opt-in snapshot it travels to teammates; it can steer host models that hold their own tools.
B.gap: No review gate or rollback for persisted ADR text and imported snapshots.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: The server loads no third-party code at runtime: its 158 language grammars, the embedding model and SQLite are compiled into the binary, SQLite extension loading is compiled out, and it installs no packages or plugins. Updates are done by the install script or a package manager, never by the running server.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: The server holds no API keys or tokens, sends nothing to any third party and has no telemetry. Its configuration scanners drop values that look like secrets before storing them in the graph, private key files are skipped during discovery, and the request log records only tool names and timings, never arguments or results. Source returned to the model is not redacted, though: search_code and get_code_snippet return whatever the files contain, and helper processes inherit the full environment.

S.finding: Secret-pattern filtering in the env and infrastructure scanners and content-free request logging in owner-only log files.
S.gap: No redaction of secrets in content returned to the model.

C.finding: Logs and the stored graph are covered; model-bound search and snippet output and subprocess environments are not.
C.gap: Model-bound results and helper environments are not filtered.

D.finding: No telemetry or crash reporting exists; diagnostics are opt-in and record only resource counters; secret filtering in scans is always on.
D.gap: Stored indexes (which contain source text) are not encrypted or minimised.

evidence.note: Hits are code comments and an OpenTelemetry trace parser; no telemetry client exists.

B.finding: Ambient-only design that accepts no key material, so there is nothing of the server's own to leak; residual exposure is repository content returned to the host model.

evidence.note: No outbound client; the server takes no API key.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: Every tool call handled by the shared daemon is logged with the tool name, error status and duration to an owner-only log file in the user's cache folder, outside the indexed repository. The log does not record arguments, the project acted on or which client asked, so it cannot show what a call actually did. The file is capped at 5 MB with one rotated copy, and logging failures do not stop actions.

S.finding: Structured per-call log lines carry the tool name, status and duration but no arguments or target.
S.gap: No arguments, target project or requesting client in the record.

C.finding: All tool calls pass through the one dispatcher that logs them; there are no extensions or sub-agents.
C.gap: Index writes, ADR changes and deletions are not recorded with their details.

D.finding: On by default at the daemon's info level and written to the cache log directory, outside the workspace; the server process could still alter it.
D.gap: The record is written by the same process it describes.

B.finding: Best-effort logging with a 5 MB cap and a single rotated copy; actions proceed if logging fails.
B.gap: Records are not durable per action and cannot replay a trajectory.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: The server bounds most of its own work: Cypher queries and code searches stop after 30 seconds, traversal limits and snippet sizes are clamped to hard ceilings, and in-flight indexing and searches can be cancelled when the client goes away. Indexing size limits are off by default, the stdio bridge waits up to 24 hours for a request, and asynchronous index jobs and the background watcher keep running until the shared daemon stops.

S.finding: Server-enforced wall-clock deadlines on queries and searches, output caps on traces and snippets, and cancellation of in-flight requests.
S.gap: Not every operation is capped (index size limits default to off) and there are no rate limits on tool calls.

C.finding: Deadlines cover the query and search paths and their helper processes; background watcher re-indexing and async index jobs run outside those per-call limits.
C.gap: Background and async work does not count against a shared budget.

evidence.contains: Register background git watcher on session connect

critical_findings.summary: Helper git, grep and find commands are built as shell strings that include model-supplied values, guarded only by a character filter, and run unsandboxed as the user with the inherited environment.

rule_of_two.sensitive_data: Any user-readable directory outside the denied roots can be indexed and read (src/foundation/workspace.c:332)
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: Local writes only: manage_adr, delete_project, index persistence (src/mcp/mcp.c:859); no egress

fixes.summary: Run git, grep and find helpers through the existing argv-based subprocess API with a minimal environment instead of /bin/sh command strings.
Require a content-keyed trust approval (as already done for the roots manifest) before importing a repository-supplied graph snapshot, and keep ADR history so changes can be reviewed and rolled back.
Log each tool call's arguments (or a redacted digest), target project and requesting client alongside the existing name and status.
Add a preview or dry-run mode for delete_project and ADR replacement.
Make the read-only analysis profile the default for the main MCP entry and expose write tools only on explicit opt-in.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.
The installer (45 client integrations in src/cli) was reviewed only for auto-approve or permission grants and the hook design; per-client config writers were not audited line by line.

The opt-in graph UI HTTP server was reviewed only for its default (off), loopback binding and origin checks; Windows-specific command paths, the vendored tree-sitter grammars, SQLite and the LSP resolution passes were not examined.
No attempts to steer AI reviewers were found in the files read.
